t: Heaters — Minimum Radius to Cover All Houses
o: We must pick one radius R so that every house lies within distance R of at least one heater, minimizing R. For each house, the best heater is its nearest heater; the answer is the maximum over houses of that nearest-heater distance. In Example 1 (houses [1,2,3], heaters [2]), the farthest house from the heater is at distance 1, so R = 1. In Example 2 (houses [1,2,3,4], heaters [1,4]), each house has a heater within distance 1. In Example 3 (houses [1,5], heater [2]), house 5 is at distance 3, so R = 3. With n up to 3·10^4, an O(n log n) approach after sorting is easily fast enough; a naive O(n·m) scan of all heaters per house would be ~9·10^8 in the worst case and risks TLE.
k: The answer equals max over houses of the distance to that house's nearest heater — each house only cares about its closest heater.
Sort both arrays; then for each house, binary search the heaters array to find the nearest heater on either side in O(log m).
Alternatively, sort both arrays and sweep with two pointers: since both are sorted, the candidate heater index only moves forward.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort + Binary Search per House
a.i: For each house, find where it would sit among the sorted heaters using binary search. The nearest heater is either the first heater ≥ the house or the last heater < it; take the minimum of those two distances. The answer is the maximum such distance over all houses. This directly computes the minimal radius needed.
s: For each house h, binary search heaters for the insertion point i.
Candidate distances: |h - heaters[i]| if i exists, and |h - heaters[i-1]| if i > 0.
Track the maximum of the minimum candidate over all houses; return it.
a.t: O(n log n + m log m) — sorting both arrays dominates; each of the n houses does an O(log m) binary search.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond sorting (or O(sort) depending on the language's sort implementation).

a.n: Approach 2: Sort Both + Two Pointers Sweep
a.i: After sorting both arrays, walk through houses left to right while advancing a pointer j into the heaters array. For house h, advance j while the next heater is not farther than the current one; then the radius for this house is min(|h - heaters[j]|, |h - heaters[j+1]|) when j+1 exists. Since both sequences are sorted, j never moves backward, giving linear time after sorting.
s: For each house h, advance j while j+1 < m and |heaters[j+1] - h| <= |heaters[j] - h|.
Update ans = max(ans, |heaters[j] - h|); also consider heaters[j+1] if it exists.
a.t: O(n log n + m log m) — sorting dominates; the two-pointer sweep is O(n + m) since j only advances.

w: In an interview, lead with the key observation that the answer is the maximum nearest-heater distance, then present the two-pointer solution as optimal (simplest code, single pass after sorting); mention binary search as an equally valid alternative. Common pitfalls: forgetting to sort both arrays (the input order is arbitrary), off-by-one errors when the house sits exactly on a heater or before all heaters, and integer overflow when computing differences in Java/C++ (positions up to 10^9, so use long/long long or rely on subtraction staying within int range carefully). Edge cases: a single house or single heater, duplicate positions, and houses outside the range spanned by heaters. Likely follow-ups: what if heaters had different radii (binary search on answer still works), or if you could add one new heater (try each gap between consecutive sorted points).
